qt: to the Commission Stanisław Tyszka (ESN) Subject:

The EU Agency for Fundamental Rights (FRA) collects comprehensive data on the origin of migrants and their descendants in order to conduct research on discrimination. In 2022, it looked at over 16 000 people from selected migrant groups, comparing the results by country of origin and generation, among other factors. Meanwhile, Eurostat’s statistics on suspects and offenders distinguish between nationals of a given country and non‑nationals. They do not show the country of birth or the parents’ country of origin, and they do not link this information to the type of offence. Naturalised migrants are classified as nationals, which makes it difficult to reliably assess the impact that migration has on security. Sweden has shown that a more detailed analysis is possible. By linking national registers, it has assessed suspects by country of birth, parents’ country of origin, age, gender and type of offence. The Swedish National Council for Crime Prevention has found that such research reduces guesswork and speculation. 1.
Why do the Commission apply double standards by looking in detail at the origins of migrants as victims of discrimination, but not at their involvement in crime?

In the Commission’s view, do the data from Eurostat allow for a reliable assessment of the impact that migration has on security, even though they do not take into account the country of birth, the parents’ country of origin or the type of offence?

What steps will the Commission take – and within what time frame – to ensure that Eurostat, in cooperation with the Member States, starts collecting comparable data covering this information, as well as details on and age and gender?
